questions.question: Layered vs Hexagonal vs Clean vs Onion architecture — what's the real difference and which to choose?
questions.title: Layered vs Hexagonal vs Clean vs Onion Architecture
questions.direct_answer: All four are attempts to decouple business logic from delivery and infrastructure — they share 90% of the philosophy and differ in emphasis: **Layered (N-tier)** is the classic controller→service→repository; dependencies flow downward; simplest but can't enforce 'domain doesn't know about DB'. **Hexagonal (Ports & Adapters, Alistair Cockburn)** puts domain at center; ports define contracts, adapters implement them; very explicit about inbound vs outbound dependencies. **Onion (Jeffrey Palermo)** is hexagonal with explicit concentric rings; dependencies point inward; domain model at core. **Clean Architecture (Uncle Bob)** is onion with more opinionated layers (Entities, Use Cases, Interface Adapters, Frameworks) and the Dependency Rule. In practice, Hexagonal and Clean are near-identical; pick one vocabulary and stop debating; layered is fine for small CRUD apps.

interviewer_intent.testing: Understanding of the real goals of these patterns; recognizing they overlap heavily
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Treating them as rigidly different; religious wars about terminology; over-engineering a simple CRUD app with clean architecture
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Discuss the Dependency Inversion Principle as the core idea; why dependency direction matters; pragmatic blending; testability as the real payoff

sections.title: Same Goal, Different Vocabularies
sections.content:
All four architectures solve the same problem: **decouple business logic from delivery mechanisms (HTTP, CLI, UI) and infrastructure (databases, message brokers, external APIs)**. They let you:
- Swap infrastructure (Postgres → DynamoDB) without changing business logic
- Test business logic without spinning up Spring, database, or HTTP
- Change UI or API (REST → gRPC) without touching domain
- Express the domain in the language of the business, not technical plumbing

The difference is emphasis and terminology.

**Layered (N-tier) Architecture** — the classic
Controller → Service → Repository → Database. Dependencies flow downward (controller depends on service; service on repository; repository on DB). Simple, familiar. The weakness: upper layers can't easily be unaware of lower layers. A service imports a `JpaRepository`; that JpaRepository's existence couples the service to JPA/Hibernate. Layered doesn't enforce dependency direction reversal.

**Hexagonal (Ports & Adapters)** — Alistair Cockburn, 2005
Domain is central. It defines **ports** (interfaces) for everything it needs: 'I need to save an order', 'I need to send an email'. **Adapters** (REST controller, JPA repository, SMTP sender) implement those ports. Inbound adapters drive the domain (HTTP → Use Case); outbound adapters serve the domain (Use Case → Database). The domain knows only about ports; never adapters. Clear separation.

**Onion Architecture** — Jeffrey Palermo, 2008
Concentric rings: Domain Model at center, then Domain Services, then Application Services, then Infrastructure at the outside. The rule: **dependencies point inward**. Outer rings know inner; inner rings don't know outer. Very explicit diagram; basically hexagonal with more layers.

**Clean Architecture** — Robert C. Martin (Uncle Bob), 2012
Layered concentric rings: Entities (enterprise business rules) → Use Cases (application rules) → Interface Adapters (controllers, gateways, presenters) → Frameworks & Drivers. Same Dependency Rule as Onion. Adds explicit categories (Entity, Use Case, Gateway, Presenter).

**Are they really different?**

Hexagonal, Onion, and Clean are substantially the same idea with different diagrams and vocabularies. The core: **business logic at center; dependencies point inward; infrastructure is a plugin**. Layered is the odd one out — it doesn't invert dependencies by default.

In 2026, the useful way to think: **pick a vocabulary (hexagonal is common in Spring Boot), follow the Dependency Inversion Principle, and stop debating terminology**.

sections.title: The Key Differences Summarized
sections.content:
| Dimension | Layered | Hexagonal | Onion | Clean |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Core idea** | Stack of layers | Ports (contracts) + Adapters (impls) | Concentric rings, dependencies inward | Same as Onion + specific categories |
| **Dependency direction** | Top to bottom | Outside to center | Outside to center | Outside to center |
| **DI of infrastructure** | Optional | Mandatory | Mandatory | Mandatory |
| **Domain isolation** | Weak | Strong | Strong | Strong |
| **Explicit use cases** | Not required | Implicit | Application Services | Use Cases (explicit layer) |
| **Inbound vs outbound** | Not distinguished | Explicit (left vs right) | Part of outer ring | Part of Interface Adapters |
| **Terminology burden** | Low | Low-Medium | Medium | High |
| **Fit for simple CRUD** | Yes | Overkill | Overkill | Overkill |
| **Fit for complex domain** | Weak | Excellent | Excellent | Excellent |
| **DDD alignment** | Poor | Good | Excellent | Excellent |
| **Spring Boot idiomatic** | Very (default) | Yes | Yes | Yes |
| **Popular in** | Everywhere | DDD, microservices | DDD communities | Uncle Bob fans, mobile apps |

sections.title: Concrete Code Example: Same Feature, Three Ways
When to Use Each + Pragmatic Reality
sections.content:
**Layered is fine for:**
- Simple CRUD apps (admin panel, internal tool)
- Early-stage startups where speed > purity
- Small teams / single-author code
- Less than ~10 use cases total
- Business logic is thin (mostly CRUD + validation)

**Upgrade to hexagonal when:**
- Domain has real business rules (invariants, workflows)
- Multiple delivery mechanisms (REST + gRPC + scheduled job)
- Multiple infrastructure integrations
- Testing is expensive (need to mock Spring/JPA)
- Want to swap Postgres → DynamoDB or Stripe → Adyen
- Team practices DDD

**Clean Architecture specifically when:**
- You want explicit categories (Use Case classes, not 'Service')
- Mobile apps (Uncle Bob's book targeted mobile/embedded)
- Regulated domains needing separation for audit

**Hexagonal vs Clean in practice:**

Near-identical in Spring Boot code. Hexagonal emphasizes ports + adapters vocabulary. Clean emphasizes use cases + entities. Pick one; don't fight about it.

**Common pitfalls:**

*Anemic domain model*
- Entities are just data holders; all logic in services
- Symptom of procedural thinking dressed up as OO
- Fix: put behavior on entities ('order.cancel()' not 'orderService.cancel(order)')

*Leaky abstractions*
- Domain port returns `Page<Order>` (Spring Data type)
- Fix: domain returns `List<Order>` + separate pagination metadata

*Over-engineering simple CRUD*
- 'Create user' use case with ports, adapters, DTOs, mappers
- 10 files for 10 lines of logic
- Fix: stay layered for simple; upgrade selectively

*DTO explosion*
- RestDto ↔ Command ↔ Domain ↔ Entity ↔ ResponseDto, all needing mappers
- MapStruct helps but still boilerplate
- Fix: use domain model in inbound/outbound boundaries where safe; mappers only where needed

*DI framework coupling in domain*
- Put `@Service` on domain use case
- Domain now depends on Spring
- Fix: plain classes; Spring config module wires them

*Circular dependencies*
- Use case A calls use case B calls use case A
- Refactor: extract shared logic to domain service or events

**DDD alignment**
- Layered: weak; CRUD-driven, not domain-driven
- Hexagonal / Onion / Clean: excellent; ports isolate domain; aggregates, repositories, domain services fit naturally

**Microservices fit.** Each microservice is its own hexagonal mini-app. Shared libraries for common domain types (Money, TenantId) are OK; resist sharing use cases.

**Modular monolith fit.** Each module is hexagonal; ports between modules cross via events or in-process interfaces. Modular monolith is often better than microservices until organizational scale demands it.

**Testing payoff is real.**
- Layered: unit tests need Spring context or heavy mocking
- Hexagonal: use cases unit-test with fake ports (`FakeOrderRepository`); no Spring, no DB; milliseconds
- Integration tests verify adapters separately

**Build-time enforcement.** Tools like ArchUnit, Modulith can enforce 'domain cannot import adapter classes'. Prevents architectural drift in large teams.

**Performance.** No runtime cost; architectural patterns are compile-time concerns.

**Learning curve.** Hexagonal adds some ceremony; juniors may struggle. Invest in documentation and examples.

**The pragmatic recommendation:**
1. **Default to hexagonal (ports + adapters) for new microservices**
2. **Stay layered for simple CRUD until domain complexity warrants upgrade**
3. **Don't argue about Hexagonal vs Clean vs Onion terminology**; pick one, document, move on
4. **Enforce with ArchUnit**; measure with actual test independence
5. **Use DDD tactical patterns** (aggregates, repositories, domain services) within whichever architecture
6. **Package by feature, not by layer** (e.g., `com.example.order`, not `com.example.controllers`)

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **All four solve the same problem**: decouple business logic from delivery + infrastructure
- **Layered (N-tier)**: simplest; dependencies flow downward; fine for CRUD; doesn't enforce inversion
- **Hexagonal (Ports & Adapters)**: domain at center; ports define contracts; adapters implement
- **Onion**: concentric rings; dependencies point inward
- **Clean Architecture**: Onion with explicit Entity/UseCase/Adapter/Framework categories
- **Hexagonal and Clean are near-identical** in Spring Boot; pick vocabulary and move on
- **Dependency Inversion Principle** is the real idea; business logic shouldn't depend on infrastructure
- **Anemic domain model** is a common anti-pattern; put behavior on entities
- **Don't over-engineer** simple CRUD apps with ports and adapters
- **ArchUnit enforces** architectural boundaries at compile/test time
- **Package by feature** (by bounded context), not by technical layer

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
All four architectures are attempts to solve the same problem: decouple business logic from delivery mechanisms and infrastructure. They differ in vocabulary and emphasis, not fundamental goal.

**The common goal**
- Swap infrastructure without changing business logic
- Test business logic without spinning up Spring or databases
- Change UI or API without touching domain
- Express the domain in business language, not technical plumbing

**The four approaches**

*Layered (N-tier) — the classic*
- Controller, Service, Repository, Database
- Dependencies flow downward
- Simple, familiar, Spring Boot's default
- Weakness: doesn't enforce dependency inversion; services directly import JpaRepository, JavaMailSender
- Swapping infrastructure requires rewriting business layer

*Hexagonal (Ports and Adapters) — Alistair Cockburn, 2005*
- Domain at center
- Ports are interfaces the domain defines
- Adapters implement the ports
- Inbound adapters drive the domain (HTTP, CLI)
- Outbound adapters serve the domain (JPA, SMTP)
- Domain knows only ports; never adapters

*Onion — Jeffrey Palermo, 2008*
- Concentric rings: Entities, Domain Services, Application Services, Infrastructure
- Rule: dependencies point inward
- Very explicit diagram; essentially hexagonal with more layers

*Clean Architecture — Uncle Bob, 2012*
- Onion with explicit categories: Entities, Use Cases, Interface Adapters, Frameworks
- Same Dependency Rule as Onion
- More opinionated vocabulary

**Are they really different?**
- Hexagonal, Onion, Clean are substantially the same
- Core idea: business logic at center, dependencies point inward, infrastructure is a plugin
- Layered is the odd one out; doesn't invert dependencies
- In 2026, pick vocabulary (hexagonal is common in Spring Boot), follow Dependency Inversion Principle, stop debating terminology

**The Dependency Inversion Principle is the real idea**
- Business logic doesn't depend on infrastructure
- Both depend on abstractions (interfaces)
- The interfaces are owned by the business logic, not the infrastructure

**When to pick each**

*Layered when*
- Simple CRUD app
- Small team, single developer
- Less than 10 use cases total
- Business logic thin
- Speed over purity

*Hexagonal when*
- Domain has real business rules
- Multiple delivery mechanisms (REST + gRPC + scheduled job)
- Multiple infrastructure integrations
- Testing expensive with Spring/JPA
- Team practices DDD

*Clean Architecture when*
- Want explicit Use Case classes
- Mobile apps (Uncle Bob's original target)
- Regulated domains needing separation for audit

**Common pitfalls**

*Anemic domain model*
- Entities are just data holders; all logic in services
- Procedural thinking dressed up as OO
- Put behavior on entities: 'order.cancel()' not 'orderService.cancel(order)'

*Leaky abstractions*
- Domain port returns Spring Data Page type
- Fix: return domain List plus separate pagination metadata

*Over-engineering CRUD*
- 'Create user' with ports, adapters, DTOs, mappers
- 10 files for 10 lines of logic
- Stay layered when complexity doesn't warrant it

*DI framework coupling in domain*
- Putting @Service on domain class
- Domain now depends on Spring
- Plain classes; Spring config module wires them

*DTO explosion*
- RestDto, Command, Domain, Entity, ResponseDto all with mappers
- MapStruct helps but still boilerplate
- Use domain at boundaries where safe; mappers only where needed

**Package structure matters**
- Package by feature, not by technical layer
- com.example.order, not com.example.controllers
- Bounded contexts align with packages

**Enforcement tools**
- ArchUnit checks 'domain cannot import adapter classes' at test time
- Prevents drift in large teams
- Spring Modulith enforces module boundaries

**Testing payoff is real**
- Layered: unit tests need Spring context or heavy mocking
- Hexagonal: use cases unit-test with fake ports; no Spring, no DB; milliseconds
- Integration tests verify adapters separately

**DDD alignment**
- Layered: weak; CRUD-driven
- Hexagonal, Onion, Clean: excellent; aggregates, repositories, domain services fit naturally

**Microservices and modular monoliths**
- Each microservice is its own hexagonal mini-app
- Modular monolith: each module is hexagonal
- Modular monolith often better than microservices until organizational scale demands

**The pragmatic recommendation**
- Default to hexagonal for new microservices
- Stay layered for simple CRUD
- Don't argue about Hexagonal vs Clean vs Onion
- Enforce with ArchUnit
- Use DDD tactical patterns within whichever architecture
- Package by feature, not layer

**The strategic answer**
- All four share the same core idea: domain at center, infrastructure as plugin
- Pick vocabulary that fits your team
- Test independence is the real payoff
- Don't over-engineer simple apps; don't under-engineer complex ones
- Business logic that runs without Spring is the gold standard
